item.title: Effect of airway assistant training on intubation time during simulated prehospital airway management: A pilot study
item.description:
Objectives: Challenging airways are common in the out-of-hospital setting, where delays or failure to secure the airway can result in significant morbidity and mortality. Therefore, this pilot study aimed to determine whether training paramedics in the role of airway assistant improves intubation time during a simulated regurgitating airway using suction-assisted laryngoscopy and airway decontamination (SALAD).

Methods: Twelve qualified paramedics were randomly allocated to one of two groups (n = 6) and paired with intensive care paramedics (ICPs). Airway assistants in Group 1 completed a one-hour airway assistant training program, whereas airway assistants in Group 2 received no training. Participants completed a standardized, timed simulation using a continuously regurgitating mannequin designed to replicate the challenges of out-of-hospital intubation. The primary outcome was time to successful intubation, defined as passage of the endotracheal tube through the vocal cords with cuff inflation.

Results: Airway assistant training significantly reduced intubation time. The untrained group recorded a median intubation time of 102.5 seconds (IQR 36), compared with 53 seconds (IQR 19) in the trained group. Group comparisons demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in intubation time (p = 0.009) and corresponded to a very large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.86; Hedges' g = 1.72). No association was observed between intubation time and the age or experience of either the airway assistant or the ICP. No esophageal intubations occurred in either group.

Conclusions: In this pilot study, training paramedics to perform the airway assistant role significantly reduced intubation time in a simulated regurgitating airway. These preliminary findings suggest that incorporating structured airway assistant training into prehospital education programs may improve airway management performance in challenging environments. Given the small sample size and simulated setting, larger studies are required to confirm these findings and determine whether the observed benefits translate to clinical practice.

Bogaerts C, Micalos PS, Deravin LM

item.title: Prehospital Advanced Airway Management in Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Cohort Study Using Time-Dependent Propensity Score Sequential Matching
item.description:
Objectives: Traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (TCA) has extremely poor outcomes, and the benefit of prehospital advanced airway management (AAM) remains uncertain, partly because previous observational studies may have been affected by resuscitation time bias. We examined the association between prehospital AAM and clinical outcomes in adults with TCA using a time-dependent analytic approach.

Methods: We conducted a nationwide retrospective observational cohort study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry linked with emergency medical services transport records from 2021 to 2023. Adults (≥18 years) with TCA were included. The exposure was successful prehospital AAM, including supraglottic airway placement or endotracheal intubation. The primary outcome was 30-day survival, and the secondary outcome was favorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2) at 30 days. We applied time-dependent propensity score sequential matching and estimated corrected risk differences (RDs) using generalized estimating equations with inverse-frequency weighting.

Results: Among 7,217 patients, 2,653 (36.8%) received prehospital AAM, of whom 2,637 were successfully matched within the analytic cohort. Thirty-day survival was 1.8% in the AAM group and 1.4% among matched controls (corrected RD, 0.6%; 95% confidence interval (CI), -0.1 to 1.2). Favorable neurological outcome occurred in 0.2% and 0.4%, respectively (corrected RD, -0.2%; 95% CI, -0.6 to 0.1). No significant timing-dependent association or prespecified subgroup heterogeneity was observed.

Conclusions: In this nationwide cohort study using time-dependent propensity score sequential matching, prehospital AAM was not significantly associated with improved outcomes in adults with TCA.

Shiozumi T, Shimomura Y, Matsuyama T, Komukai S, Shida H, Tanaka A

item.title: Pooled prevalence of infectious diseases among first responders in the prehospital setting: A systematic review with meta-analysis by occupation
item.description:
Objectives: First responders often work in unpredictable, uncontrolled environments, where exposure to infected patients and contaminated environments heighten the risk of communicable disease transmission. Their higher infection prevalence compared with the general population has driven the implementation of personal protective equipment, vaccination requirements, safety protocols, and infection prevention education. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of infections among first responders in the prehospital workers including paramedics, emergency medical technicians, patient transport staff, firefighters, police, and police officers.

Methods: Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science and PUBMED/Medline were systematically searched. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation, with Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation and back-transformation to the original prevalence scale. Heterogeneity was assessed using I², τ², and 95% prediction intervals. Meta-regression was used to examine potential sources of between-study heterogeneity, and small-study effects and potential publication bias were assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression test. Risk of bias was investigated using the AXIS tool.

Results: Following the initial search, 34,874 articles were identified, of which 88 were full-text screened. Of these, 22 studies representing 19,188 first responders were included in this systematic review. The pooled prevalences of hepatitis B and C were 6.2% (95% CI 4.5%-8.2%) and 1.8% (95% CI 0.9%-2.9%), respectively. Around 4% (95% CI 2.6%- 5.9%) of the first responders had MRSA colonisation. Current or past infection with COVID-19 among non-vaccinated first responders was 13.6% (95% CI 4.8%- 25.9%), which reduced to 7.3% (95% CI 3.6%- 12%) after exclusion of studies with high risk of bias. Of the known study characteristics, geographic region significantly contributed to heterogeneity, explaining 36.7% of between-study variance, p = 0.039.

Conclusions: Infectious disease prevalence varied across pathogens, occupations, and geographical settings among first responders. These findings should be interpreted in light of substantial heterogeneity and limitations in the available evidence but may help inform infection prevention, occupational health policy, vaccination strategies, and future research in first responder services.

Alahmari H, Hanson L, Kelley P, Harris K, Spong J, Milazzo A

item.title: Prehospital Whole Blood Resuscitation in Pediatric Patients: A San Antonio Cohort Descriptive
item.description:
Objectives: The objective of this study is to describe the demographic, clinical, and prehospital care characteristics of pediatric patients receiving whole blood (WB) resuscitation by San Antonio Fire Department (SAFD).

Methods: We conducted an observational retrospective cohort study to evaluate pediatric patients who received prehospital low-titer group O positive WB transfusion through the SAFD prehospital blood program between October 2018 and June 2025. The objective was to characterize patient demographics, injury patterns, resuscitative interventions, shock physiology, and outcomes among pediatric recipients in a mature civilian emergency medical services WB program.

Results: Of 1703 WB transfusions, 73 (4.3%) were pediatric. Most patients were male (76%), age range 1-17 years old with a mode of 17 years, adolescents represented 78%. Trauma accounted for 96% of cases, firearm injury (74%); all penetrating (84%), blunt (12%), with the remainder classified as medical/unknown. Vascular access was intravenous (73%), intraosseous (26%). Tranexamic acid was co-administered in 39%; 12% received ceftriaxone. When analyzed using age-adjusted Shock Index Pediatric Age-Adjusted (SIPA) thresholds (>1.2 for 1-6 years, >1.0 for 7-12 years, and >0.9 for 13-17 years), based on the initial available prehospital heart rate and systolic blood pressure, 45% of patients had an elevated SIPA, 22% had a normal SIPA, 20% were pulseless and therefore could not undergo SIPA calculation, and 14% lacked sufficient vital-sign data for classification. Survival was 50%; died 39%, and unknown outcomes 11%. Mean delta shock index values were most negative in toddlers (1-4 years) -0.97 ± 1.29, followed by children (5-11 years) -0.76 ± 1.07 and adolescents (12-17 years) -0.16 ± 0.46, indicating a greater physiologic response to resuscitation among younger pediatric patients.

Conclusions: Pediatric WB recipients were predominantly adolescent males who sustained penetrating trauma and presented with moderate-to-severe shock. Younger age groups had larger descriptive decreases in shock index during the prehospital encounter; however, these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small subgroup sizes and observational design.

Danboise B, Dieterle M, Bullock W, Wampler D, Winckler C

item.title: Emergency Response and Patient Transport in Remote Indigenous Communities: A Scoping Review
item.description:
Objectives: Prehospital and inter-facility transport, such as air medical retrieval and pre-birth evacuation, often move Indigenous patients in rural and remote settings out of their communities, where care is already shaped by fragmented funding and structural inequities; no review has mapped these pathways globally. This scoping review mapped evidence on prehospital emergency response and patient transport for this population.

Methods: A librarian-assisted PubMed, Embase, and Scopus search was conducted for English-language publications on March 9, 2026. Eligible studies included an explicit rural Indigenous population with a defined prehospital pathway. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed full texts, and a third reviewer resolved disagreements. Data were charted using a standardized form and synthesized descriptively.

Results: Across eight countries, 76 studies met the inclusion criteria, primarily from Australia (n = 29) and Canada (n = 23). Air transport and medical evacuation was the most frequently described pathway (71%), followed by ground transport (51%). Explicit description of paramedic or emergency medical services (24%) and dispatch/9-1-1 (12%) were depicted less frequently. Additionally, pathways were commonly described but rarely evaluated: only 12/76 (16%) publications used an evaluative design, and no pathway was evaluated in more than 7 of 76 publications (9%). The most reported barriers were infrastructure and communications (92%), cost and jurisdiction (87%), and distance to definitive care (83%). All percentages describe how often a topic was reported across the 76 included publications, and not its prevalence in practice. An explicit cultural-safety framework was applied in 9% of the publications, and community-led governance of the research in 7%.

Conclusions: The published evidence disproportionately described transporting patients out of their communities. Community first response and tele-support were described more often than their standing in the literature suggests; however, they were rarely evaluated, and Indigenous-led governance of the research itself was reported in 7% of publications. Low reporting frequency does not establish that these models are uncommon in application and practice. Future priorities include community-partnered evaluation of community-based capacity and telehealth-supported care, alongside the development of patient and family cultural safety.

Lee CPS, Barron L, Mian H
